new_statements.quote: Alex (1989:24) remarks that “all Central Delta lects operate a basic two-tone system”. These tones are low tone, which is marked with a grave accent ( ̀ ), and high tone, which is marked with an acute accent ( ´ ). There is also a downstep phenomenon in these languages. The downstep is marked with a small arrow pointing downwards ( ꜜ ) between two high-toned syllables. Apart from the syllabic nasal, tone in these languages is anchored on vowels. Table 7 shows these tones and downstep as found in Abuan, Oḍual and Ogbrọnụagum.

The quoted passage is at p. 11, sec. 3.4 'Tone' (txt lines 559-566) and matches word for word: 'Alex (1989:24) remarks that "all Central Delta lects operate a basic two-tone system". These tones are low tone... grave accent... high tone... acute accent... downstep... marked with a small arrow pointing downwards ( ꜜ) between two high-toned syllables. Apart from the syllabic nasal, tone in these languages is anchored on vowels. Table 7 shows these tones and downstep as found in Abuan, Odual and Ogbronuagum.' grep confirms 0 occurrences of 'stress' in the whole paper; 'accent' occurs only as the names of the ton…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Ogbogolo, like all Central Delta languages, is treated as a two-level tone language (H, L) with downstep; every vowel (and syllabic nasal) bears tone. No source seen says anything about word stress or accent placement in Ogbogolo.
new_statements.exceptions: None; the tone statement is a family-level generalisation illustrated only with Abuan, Odual and Ogbronuagum forms, not Ogbogolo forms.
new_statements.domain_note: Lexical and grammatical tone (word level); the statement is second-hand (Kari quoting Alex 1989) and generic to Central Delta, applied to Ogbogolo by membership. Nothing on citation-form prominence or phrase-level accent.
new_statements.identity_note: All sources refer to the same single-town language Ogbogolo/Obogolo (ogbo1242, ISO ogg), Ahoada West LGA, Rivers State (Blench 2008; Kari 2017 Table 3 instead gives 'Bayelsa State: Yenagoa LGA', apparently an error carried from Ethnologue mapping). The quoted tone statement is a Central Delta family-level generalisation (Kari 2017 quoting Alex 1989), not an Ogbogolo-specific observation, and it says nothing about stress.

sources.note: Nothing: the word 'stress' does not occur in the paper. Sec. 3 (phonological overview) covers vowels, consonants (Ogbogolo credited with 27 consonants after Olibie 1994 / Francstan 1995), syllable structure and, in sec. 3.4 (p. 11), tone: quoting Alex (1989:24) that 'all Central Delta lects operate a basic two-tone system' (H, L) plus downstep, tone anchored on vowels and syllabic nasals; tone examples given only for Abuan, Odual and Ogbronuagum. Ogbogolo data throughout are second-hand from two unpublished UniPort long essays.
Bibliography only: MEDs = Francstan 1995, Olibie 1994 (phonology_or_text), Thomas 1914 (wordlist).
